extracted.intended_audience: cartoonists, humor writers, scholars and readers interested in Charles Schulz, Peanuts, and psychological/melancholic humor
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for crafting character-driven, psychologically complex comic strips in the style of Charles Schulz's Peanuts: focus on unresolved interior problems, recurring gags, understated drawing and precise timing that lets humor coexist with melancholy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Philosophy — "Happiness is not funny at all."
rubrics_metrics.description: "Happiness is not funny at all." Misery became Schulz's strategy. Peanuts is about people working out the interior problems of daily lives WITHOUT ever solving them — the absence of solution is the center of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center strips on interior conflict and dissatisfaction rather than neat resolutions; let the lack of solution be the comedic engine. Avoid punchlines that resolve the emotional problem—the humor comes from continued struggle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Are characters working through interior problems?
rubrics_metrics.description: Are characters working through interior problems?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be engaged in trying to manage or articulate psychological, philosophical, or sociological dilemmas (small daily anxieties, existential worries) rather than only surface jokes. The strip's action should reflect inner life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Are problems left unresolved (stays funny because uncured)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Are problems left unresolved (stays funny because uncured)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep recurring situations open-ended across strips so the tension and humor persist. Avoid tidy solutions; the comedic value often depends on repetition and lack of catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the recurring failure dignified rather than cruel?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the recurring failure dignified rather than cruel?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame characters' repeated defeats with empathy and dignity—comic pathos rather than mean-spirited humiliation. Readers should feel recognition and sympathy (dignity in defeat), not simple ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does it tackle taboo emotional themes?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it tackle taboo emotional themes?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address subjects often considered off-limits for comics—faith, intolerance, depression, loneliness, cruelty, despair, failure, persistence—while maintaining subtlety. Use these themes to add depth, not shock value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does humor coexist with melancholy?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance wit with an undercurrent of sadness or longing. Let jokes carry emotional weight; the strip should allow melancholy and humor to be simultaneous, producing gentle poignancy rather than pure cheer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of adult assumptions — child's perspective amplified
rubrics_metrics.description: A child's pain is MORE intensely felt than an adult's. A child's defeats more acutely experienced. Schulz gave kids lifelong dissatisfactions ("the stuff of which adulthood is made").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write from a child's viewpoint that treats small losses as existential, thereby revealing universal adult truths. Subvert adult presumptions by treating children's inner lives with seriousness and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style elements — spare line, timing, subtle gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: Spare pen line. Jack Benny timing. Subtle sense of humor. Tiny gestures, big meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use economical drawing and precise timing; rely on minimal visuals and understated beats. Small physical or textual gestures should carry disproportionate emotional or comic meaning—avoid over-explaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring comic engines / running gags
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurring Comic Engines: Charlie Brown's failed kite-flying. Lucy yanking the football. Snoopy's WWI Flying Ace. Linus's blanket and theology. Schroeder's piano and Beethoven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop repeatable scenarios or motifs that can be varied over time; the humor accrues through repetition and variation. Use consistent character obsessions or props as ongoing sources of comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition / relatability — 'we've all been Charlie Brown'
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition: we've all been Charlie Brown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for universal, relatable emotions so readers identify with characters' small defeats and persistent hope. The strip's authority comes from its ability to reflect common human feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hope in spite of evidence / the cosmic joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Hope in spite of evidence. The cosmic joke: trying anyway.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a thread of perseverance or optimism even when circumstances suggest futility; this tension between effort and likely failure produces bittersweet humor. Avoid nihilism—keep some humane resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channel personal struggle into the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Schulz battled clinical depression throughout life. Channeled struggles into Charlie Brown's world. "Inner gloom was also the source of his outward light."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw on sincere personal feelings or struggles to inform characters and tone—authentic vulnerability can fuel both pathos and comedy. Be careful to transform pain into art rather than exploit it gratuitously.
